title: Volvo, Candy, Pirelli: China is buying up Europe. Conspiracy or capitalism?
content:
Concerns over China’s growing economic power are particularly acute in Brussels and Washington. Yet step outside the corridors of government and onto the streets of European capitals, and it quickly becomes clear that this alarm may have come at least a decade too late. BYD showrooms are now part of the urban landscape in Warsaw, while the Chinese carmaker openly sponsors local cultural events, including open-air cinemas.

Temu and Shein parcels have become a familiar sight in European homes, while Huawei technology has long played a significant role in the continent’s telecommunications infrastructure. China has proved remarkably effective at identifying gaps in Western markets and exploiting vulnerabilities that Europe itself helped create. Crucially, it has done so while operating under an economic model fundamentally different from the traditional Western version of capitalism.

title: Slovakia delays Russia sanctions extension, seeks removal of two billionaires, journalist claims
content:
The Slovak government on Wednesday evening blocked the extension of sanctions targeting those undermining Ukraine’s territorial integrity, which apply to more than 3,000 Russian individuals and companies, according to Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda and Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL).

At the time, the EU’s Committee of Permanent Representatives (Coreper II) was discussing the extension of the sanctions, but reportedly failed to reach an agreement because of Slovakia.

Foreign media reported that Slovakia is insisting that the sanctions not be extended for a year, as the Irish presidency is now proposing, but only for six months, as has been the case until now.

Slovakia is also reportedly seeking to have several names removed from the sanctions list. According to information obtained by euBrief, specifically two names are at issue.

The countries have postponed the matter until 9 September for now, but they must reach an agreement by 15 September at the latest to prevent the sanctions from expiring.

title: Germany’s AfD Eyes Power: Should Europe Be Worried?
content:
Voters in Saxony-Anhalt will elect a new state parliament on Sunday, September 6. The right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) is polling above 40 percent, with a commanding lead over the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Winning the election, however, would not automatically put the AfD in power. The state premier is elected by parliament, and Germany’s mainstream parties continue to rule out forming a coalition with the AfD. The five-percent electoral threshold could therefore prove crucial.

“If the Greens or other smaller parties fail to make it into the state parliament, the number of so-called wasted votes will increase, and the AfD could potentially secure an absolute majority of seats without winning 50 percent of the vote. An AfD government is by no means a foregone conclusion, but it is no longer a far-fetched scenario,” says Dr Bruno Surdel, a political scientist at the Centre for Europe at the University of Warsaw.

Whatever happens in Saxony-Anhalt, the bigger story is how dramatically the AfD’s position in German politics has changed.

title: Europe’s veto problem: Can the EU learn to act without unanimity?
content:
For decades, unanimity in foreign policy has been both a safeguard of national sovereignty and one of the European Union’s greatest weaknesses.

It ensures that no member state can be forced to support a foreign-policy decision it considers fundamentally contrary to its national interests. At the same time, it gives every government the ability to prevent the EU from acting – even when the other 26 countries are ready to move forward.

Now France and Germany want to change that balance.

According to a letter, 11 EU member states are calling for a series of measures designed to make decision-making on foreign and security policy faster and more effective. Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Romania, Spain and Sweden have signed the document.

The letter was also circulated to the foreign ministers of the remaining EU member states, according to Italy’s ANSA news agency.

At the heart of the initiative is a proposal to make greater use of qualified majority voting (QMV) instead of unanimity in selected areas of foreign and security policy.

That may sound like a technical institutional reform. It is not.

title: Finland’s berry industry shifted from Thai pickers to Nepalese students, but exploitation remains unchecked
content:
The exploitation of foreign wild berry pickers in Finnish forests continues, and most of them still work without the security provided by an employment contract. 

Instead of Thai farmers travelling to Finland for the harvest season of blueberries and other wild berries, which was the setup for two decades and resulting in human trafficking, the work in the forests is now being carried out by foreign nationals already residing in the country. According to information acquired by Faktabaari, the workers are mostly higher education students from Nepal and elsewhere from South Asia. 

Reports from the Finnish occupational safety and health authorities and Victim Support Finland show the pickers have faced similar problems to those in previous years: they have reported low earnings after various costs have been deducted from their wages, as well as inadequate accommodation and food. Pickers have also been charged ‘entry fees’ which have not subsequently been refunded.

title: Do Ukrainian women subject to military service have to leave the EU?
content:
At the end of July, the European Union (EU) did indeed extend temporary protection for people displaced from Ukraine until the 4th of March 2028. At the same time, new applicants for temporary protection will have to be able to demonstrate that they have complied with the military obligations laid down in Ukrainian law.

“Given Ukraine’s evolving defence needs, temporary protection going forward will only be granted to those who have fulfilled their military service obligations in Ukraine,” the Council of the European Union states in its announcement. This can be demonstrated, for example, by a passport containing an exit stamp issued by the Ukrainian authorities showing that the person left Ukraine legally. A paper or electronic document confirming an exemption from military obligations or their fulfilment can also be used as evidence.

title: Is the European Comission planning to confiscate 90% of people’s wealth?
content:
Although Latvia is not among the countries mentioned in the video, one user on the social media platform X has already claimed that “the EC is looking into dekulakisation measures. So that everyone can be equal. Admirable. Let’s tighten our belts and chip in. Some 9 million [euros], not expensive”.

Kužnieks told Delfi that the claims made in the video had been checked by the Representation. The EC is not planning to freeze people’s bank accounts or confiscate 50% or 90% of their wealth, as claimed in the video. The Commission has also not identified any countries where such measures could be introduced first. Nor is the Commission proposing any measures to tax wealth.

The video circulating on social media uses a real study commissioned by the Commission, but its content is interpreted misleadingly. In 2026, the Directorate-General for Taxation and Customs Union (DG TAXUD) published a study aimed at gaining a better understanding of different wealth-related taxes, their interaction with one another and their effects. It reviews academic literature and analyses the experience of different countries with such taxes.

title: Latvia’s request for a 7 billion euro EU grant remains only an idea for now
content:
Following the publication of the article, many questions arose about whether Latvia had already requested this funding from the EU, when a decision by the EU institutions might be expected and how the money could be spent. However, as Delfi has established, Latvia has not yet discussed the allocation of such funds with EU institutions or other member states – it remains only an idea. Moreover, no meetings specifically devoted to the issue have been planned so far.

According to Politico, Kulbergs’ argument for why the EU should allocate the 7 billion euros to Latvia is that Latvia has to borrow money to ensure the security of countries that are much further from the frontline. The article states that these funds, which Latvia wants in addition to funding already earmarked for other countries, would account for almost half of the planned 15.12 billion euros in defence spending during the new EU multiannual budget period.

However, in comments to Delfi, the prime minister explained that the 7 billion euros is intended in the form of a grant, while stressing that “this is currently only at the level of an idea and discussions between all the eastern-flank countries and the EU are needed”.

title: Sprūds and Ministry of Defence offer different accounts of which “forgotten explosives” were needed for drones
content:
Andris Sprūds is now the Progressives’ lead candidate in the Vidzeme constituency in the upcoming parliamentary elections. Delfi contacted Sprūds and the Ministry of Defence (MoD) to fact-check the claim.

Andris Kulbergs made the claim while answering questions about drone incidents and the work of former Defence Minister Sprūds. Asked whether he was referring to systems purchased during Sprūds’ tenure for which the necessary munitions had not been bought, the prime minister declined to give a specific answer. “We bought the equipment, but forgot to buy the munitions,” Kulbergs said on the programme, adding that such a situation had occurred. He did not name the specific procurement, system, or institution responsible for failing to purchase the ammunition.

The MoD told Delfi that the munitions had not been forgotten. However, a dispute had arisen between the minister and the National Armed Forces (NAF) over their procurement, which had taken up valuable time.

title: “Romania is annexing Moldova”: how frightening disinformation exploded within a few hours
content:
It all began on the 24th of June, when Romania’s lower house of parliament, the Chamber of Deputies, technically deemed a bill submitted by the far-right and pro-Russian party S.O.S. România on the unification of Romania and Moldova to have been “adopted by tacit approval”. The bill stipulates that, once it enters into force, the Romanian government would be authorised to “urgently and immediately” begin negotiations with Chisinau on “completing the union with the Republic of Moldova”, Romanian news portal Digi24 explains.

Before explaining what “tacit approval” means and why such a proposal from a radical party does not have broad political support that would allow it to become law, let us turn to what happened next in the information space.

It took only a few hours for the claim that Romania had effectively begun annexing Moldova to spread like wildfire with the help of various actors and anonymous social media accounts.
